lineages.name: James Jamerson
lineages.why: Motown's bassist: melodic, syncopated lines with chromatic runs, ghost notes and open strings, plucked with one finger on a flatwound P-bass. He took the chord sheet and played what fitted the song and its lyric, and producers booked sessions around him and Benjamin.

lineages.name: Benny Benjamin
lineages.why: Played the template Motown beat, eighths on the hi-hat and four quarter notes on the snare with the bass drum answering Jamerson, on records from Money to My Girl and You Can't Hurry Love. Berry Gordy and other producers refused to record without him.

lineages.name: Holland-Dozier-Holland
lineages.why: Dozier and Brian Holland composed and produced; Eddie Holland wrote lyrics and arranged the vocals. They wrote a run of Supremes and Four Tops number ones including Where Did Our Love Go, Stop! In the Name of Love and You Can't Hurry Love.

lineages.name: Booker T. & the M.G.'s
lineages.why: The Stax house band (Al Jackson Jr., Duck Dunn, Steve Cropper, Booker T. Jones), usually with a horn section, behind Otis Redding, Sam & Dave and Wilson Pickett. Their sparse, groove-first playing set the Memphis soul standard.

name: Soul / Motown

notes.text: The Motown beat: eighth notes on the hi-hat, four quarter notes on the snare, and a bass drum in conversation with Jamerson's line; tambourine plays quarters or the backbeat, and a chopped guitar chord sits with it.
Motown's drummers played lightly and taped the snares for a tight, crisp sound; Pistol Allen owned the shuffles. Stax's Al Jackson Jr. played simple, economical grooves, even moving 2 and 4 to a tom.

Jamerson played melodic, syncopated lines with chromatic runs, inversions, ghost notes and open strings, where most soul bass stayed on roots and fifths. He plucked with one index finger ('the Hook') on a P-bass with old flatwounds and a foam mute: warm, punchy, little sustain.
Jamerson worked from chord sheets and then played what he felt fitted the song, including its lyric; shuffles such as How Sweet It Is use descending triads and blues-box shapes.

Diatonic major progressions with a turnaround (My Girl's verse I-IV and chorus I-ii7-IV-V) or dorian two-chord vamps (Grapevine i-IV7, Respect V7-IV7). A whole-step key change for the last chorus (My Girl's outro moves C to D) is a stock lift.
Call and response between lead and backing vocalists, from gospel, with a tense lead voice and improvised additions; background parts stay simple rather than elaborate.
Motown layered strings, brass, vibraphone and handclaps over the rhythm section, with charted string and horn sections; Stax put vibrant horn parts where backing vocals would go.
The Funk Brothers played head arrangements worked out in the session, with more than one guitarist, two keyboards, and separate tambourine and vibes players.
Motown mixed trebly, leaning on electronic limiting and high-frequency EQ boosts so records cut through AM radio. Stax put the vocal further back and weighted the low end.

Released modern R&B/soul masters: median -9.6 LUFS (middle half -11.2 to -8.3) in the largest survey, -12.6 in a smaller one. Reissues of 1960s singles are a different target; the range is for new releases in the style.
Singles run two and a half to three minutes; songwriting teams built them for weekly quality-control meetings where Berry Gordy could veto a release.
Kick with the front head off and blankets inside, snare taped underneath, floor tom tuned to G; a two-mic kit in a large live room gives the period drum sound.

notes.text: Melody ranges are measured, not recalled: 416 eight-bar windows from the melody tracks of 72 Lakh MIDI files labelled RnB by tagtraum, each read with the app's own Melodist arithmetic; the range is the 10th to 90th percentile, typical the median. Performed MIDI, so note lengths are as played. The share of chord tones is not measured: the files carry no chords. The label is the dataset's RnB label, which spans soul, Motown, funk and contemporary R&B.

pitfalls.text: Putting the snare only on 2 and 4 and calling it Motown. The Motown beat strikes the snare on all four quarters, doubled by tambourine.
A root-and-fifth bass. Motown's bass is a second melody with chromatic passing notes, syncopated pickups and ghost notes.
Hitting hard and ringing. The Motown drummers played lightly on taped, damped drums; the drive comes from the four-beat snare and tambourine, not volume.

progressions.text: My Girl's chorus and outro; the outro repeats it a whole step up.
Stop! In the Name of Love's chorus, starting off the tonic.
Grapevine's chorus vamp: the major IV7 is the dorian colour.

summary: Gospel-rooted popular song that combines R&B and jazz with call and response between lead and backing voices, handclaps and tambourine on the backbeat. Motown's version adds a four-beat snare, a melodic and syncopated electric bass, charted strings and horns and a trebly, limited mix; Stax's version sets the vocal further back behind horns and a heavy low end.
